note.question: When can a firm's reputation credibly commit it not to sell consumer data, and why does that commitment weaken as the number of firms grows?
note.overview: Long-lived firms and successive short-lived consumers interact in an infinite-horizon incomplete-information reputation game. Firms choose whether to sell consumer data, consumers choose information disclosure, and Markov perfect equilibria determine whether privacy protection is sustainable.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: At the start of each period, the consumer observes current beliefs about firm types and chooses how much information to reveal to each firm. Each firm recommends a personalized product and sets a price; the consumer buys if worthwhile. The firm then chooses whether to sell the consumer's data, the consumer observes a noisy aggregate signal, and beliefs update for future consumers. Consumers reveal information before firms decide whether to sell it, creating a static holdup problem.

components.label: Information structure
components.explanation: Each firm is either a rational type or a behavioral type that always sells data; consumers hold and update a common prior. A firm's public reputation state is the posterior probability that it is the behavioral, data-selling type, so a higher belief means a worse privacy reputation. Consumers observe a noisy signal of whether any data sale was detected but, in the main multifirm model, cannot identify which firm sold the data. A firm observes a signal generated by the consumer's chosen disclosure level and uses it to personalize product location and price.
